decisions.reason: Deriving the second V terminal from the selected Hero V termination does not itself change the Hero V; the source message's separate Hero V selection is already recorded.
The existing same-message Event selects the Hero V geometry but omits the explicit requirement that its terminal gesture also define the É accent.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
I actually think something fundamentally changed after our last conversation. Once we shifted from talking about what the V should look like to who it represents, I felt like we finally started designing with the same purpose. Thank you for asking those insightful questions. I think the philosophy really comes through in this round, and I appreciate how thoughtfully you translated it.

Option 2 is my favorite.

I honestly wonder if this may be the V. It feels more complete than anything we've explored so far.

The only refinement I'd still love to explore is the very end of the right arm. As my eye follows it upward, I want the gesture to finish with complete conviction rather than gradually fading away. Not longer. Not thicker. Not more curved. Just a slightly more intentional ending—as though it knows exactly where it's going.

I also realized that this termination won't only define the large V—it will ultimately define the smaller V and, even more importantly, the É accent. Because that gesture will become one of the defining signatures of the Vellvé identity, I think it's worth asking whether it expresses the same quiet confidence and sense of becoming that the brand represents.

decisions.reason: The candidate's same-message INTRODUCE already records the shared terminal intent, constraints, and application to the Hero V, second V, and É accent.
The terminal derivation does not change the second V's smaller, subordinate visual prominence.
The source decision concerns the shared V and É-accent terminal gesture, not the deferred E and L letterform construction.
The geometric terminal derivation neither resumes nor changes the deferred champagne material treatment.
The client's appreciation of the design discussion is incidental and does not change the requirement to provide rationale with review rounds.
The terminal-gesture decision does not alter or resume the deferred full-wordmark kerning requirement.
